cards.title: Write every ad as one-to-one salesmanship
cards.summary: Judge ad copy by asking whether it would help a salesman close a half-sold prospect standing in front of you.
cards.use_when: Drafting or reviewing any paid ad, product page or email where the prospect has already clicked or shown interest.

cards.title: Long copy works when it stays interesting
cards.summary: More telling produces more selling, provided the copy holds attention on something the prospect is already interested in.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product page, landing page or advertorial should be short or long-form for an interested audience.

cards.title: Frame ads around service, not buying requests
cards.summary: Ads that ask no one to buy and instead offer service convert better because buyers act to please themselves.
cards.use_when: Writing the offer framing and call to action for an ad, landing page or door-opener promotion.

cards.title: Spend most of your copy time on the headline
cards.summary: The headline selects and opens the door for the right readers; the entire return on an ad can hinge on it.
cards.use_when: Allocating copywriting time across a headline, subhead and body for an ad, landing page or PDP above-the-fold block.

cards.title: Use specificity to make claims land
cards.summary: Definitive statements with real numbers carry weight; platitudes and generalities roll off and leave no impression.
cards.use_when: Rewriting generic benefit claims on ads, PDPs or landing pages into defensible, specific statements.

cards.title: Exploit price perception and exclusivity psychology
cards.summary: Prices and group-restricted offers shape value perception independently of the underlying product.
cards.use_when: Framing price, tiered access, membership or VIP offers in ads and on site merchandising.

cards.title: Rewrite the same offer in different framings
cards.summary: An identical offer presented differently can multiply returns, so treat the framing itself as the test variable.
cards.use_when: Planning the next round of ad, landing page or email creative variants when the offer and price must stay fixed.

cards.title: Research deeply to find the keystone fact
cards.summary: Long, tedious research often yields the single fact that becomes the backbone of a winning campaign.
cards.use_when: Preparing the creative brief or angle list for a new product launch or a stalled ad account.

cards.title: Keep an enduring human-psychology checklist
cards.summary: Human nature is stable, so curiosity, price perception, belonging and self-interest remain reusable copy levers.
cards.use_when: Building a standing checklist or briefing template your team uses before shipping any ad or page.

cards.title: Reconcile headline impact with measured conversion
cards.summary: Headline-driven return changes are large in the source's account, but must be verified on your own traffic and metrics.
cards.use_when: Setting expectations and measurement discipline before running a headline or creative test on your store.

cards.title: Choose headlines that reveal interest, not conceal it
cards.summary: A headline should work like a news headline: help hurried readers pick out what interests them without misleading.
cards.use_when: Selecting among headline options for an ad, email subject line or landing page hero.

cards.title: Match copy length and detail to the interested reader
cards.summary: Once a prospect has shown interest, give them enough information to act rather than cutting to an arbitrary word count.
cards.use_when: Deciding how much detail to include on a PDP, landing page or long-form ad for a considered purchase.

cards.title: Run static-first creative volume instead of VSLs on Meta
cards.summary: Since Meta's Andromeda algorithm rewards sheer creative volume, prioritize a weekly static-ad production cadence over high-production video sales letters.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to allocate your creative budget and team time between video and static ad formats for a Meta campaign.

cards.title: Use identity triggers in ad copy instead of backend interest targeting
cards.summary: Insert a specific niche, demographic or category keyword directly into your winning ad's headline or body copy so the algorithm finds that buyer pocket for you.
cards.use_when: Preparing ad copy and targeting for a Meta campaign where you want to reach a specific customer segment without manual interest stacking.

cards.title: Clone your winning ad into hundreds of AI-generated variations
cards.summary: Feed your winning ad to an LLM and generate hundreds of micro-variations targeted to specific demographics, then let CBO pick winners.
cards.use_when: Scaling a proven Meta ad that risks fatiguing, when you need more creative supply from one winning format.

cards.title: Rescue ignored ads with a zombie campaign
cards.summary: Revive high-conviction ads that got zero spend in the main CBO by launching them in an isolated ad set to force delivery.
cards.use_when: After running a CBO clone campaign, when several creatives you believe in recorded zero or near-zero spend.

cards.title: Make ads that do not look like ads
cards.summary: Produce paid creative that matches natively consumed content in your niche so it does not read as advertising and die on arrival.
cards.use_when: Developing acquisition creative for a Meta or TikTok campaign where polished ad-looking assets are underperforming.

cards.title: Test broad targeting against interest stacking with identical creative
cards.summary: Run your best ad with no interest targeting alongside your stacked version and compare CPA after 7 days.
cards.use_when: Reviewing Meta targeting strategy when deciding whether to keep layered interest targeting or move to broad audiences.

cards.title: Write long-form copy to widen Meta's context window
cards.summary: Give the algorithm a large amount of descriptive copy about exactly who you want so it can locate those buyers.
cards.use_when: Writing ad copy for a broad-targeting Meta campaign where the creative must carry the audience definition.

cards.title: Match your best ad headline to the landing page headline
cards.summary: Mirror the top-performing ad headline, subheadline and lead-in on your landing page to fix scent and lift conversion rate.
cards.use_when: Optimizing a landing page or PDP after ads are driving clicks but conversion rate and CPA are poor.

cards.title: Retarget non-buyers with a different offer, not the same one louder
cards.summary: Serve people who did not buy a different product or service offer instead of repeating the same ad.
cards.use_when: Building retargeting campaigns for a store or service business with multiple products, to recapture non-converting traffic.

cards.title: Scale against blended ROAS and net free cash flow, not platform ROAS
cards.summary: Evaluate changes in absolute store contribution and cash requirements when higher spend lowers reported ROAS.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to increase Meta ad budget when the presenter's peers hesitate because reported ROAS or cost per lead has worsened.

cards.title: The Three-Question Copy Test (Visualize / Falsify / Distinct)
cards.summary: Run every product headline, ad line and PDP hook through three binary questions to find memorable, credible, ownable copy.
cards.use_when: You are writing or reviewing a product title, ad headline, PDP hero line, email subject or landing page hook and need a fast filter before shipping.

cards.title: Abstract-to-Concrete Zoom-In Exercise
cards.summary: Rewrite vague benefits by drilling down a two-column abstract/concrete sheet until you hit a picturable object or scenario.
cards.use_when: Your product benefits read as adjectives ('effective', 'convenient', 'premium') and you need concrete claims for ads, PDP bullets or category positioning.

cards.title: 'You Can't Talk, Only Point' — Replace Adjectives With Proof
cards.summary: Write copy by pointing at provable things (charts, objects, people, numbers) instead of using subjective adjectives.
cards.use_when: Your product page or ad is adjective-heavy ('high-quality', 'innovative') and you need provable claims, proof points or image directions.

cards.title: Write Claims a Competitor Couldn't Sign
cards.summary: Distinctiveness test: reject any line a competitor could legitimately copy and force copy back to your product's unique facts.
cards.use_when: Your product is functionally similar to competitors (appliances, supplements, apparel) and you need positioning language that separates you in ads and merchandising.

cards.title: Facts First: Ground Every Ad In A Verifiable Fact
cards.summary: Start from a checkable fact (not a number by definition) and build the ad or PDP story from it.
cards.use_when: Your creative or product page feels like opinion, hype or wallpaper and you need a truthful anchor with an internal story.

cards.title: The Who-Who-Says-What-Well Framework For Copy Briefs
cards.summary: Structure any copy task as: who you're talking to, what you have to say, and saying it well — with visual context driving the format.
cards.use_when: You are briefing a designer, freelancer or yourself before writing an ad, email, PDP hero block or landing page and need to avoid vague inputs.

cards.title: Build The Ad In Figma, Not In Word — Design And Copy Are One
cards.summary: Write the ad, landing page or newsletter directly in its final visual layout so line breaks, hierarchy and copy are judged as the reader sees them.
cards.use_when: You are producing static ads, a landing page hero, email creative or a newsletter and copy and layout decisions are being made separately.

cards.title: Pre-Visualise The Ad In Real Context (Feed, Billboard, Inbox)
cards.summary: Test stopping power by placing the creative where the buyer will actually see it, not against a blank canvas.
cards.use_when: You are approving static ad creatives, email headers or social hooks and want to know whether they grab attention in a busy feed.

cards.title: Conflict Pairing To Generate Ad Ideas (Sullivan's Line Down The Page)
cards.summary: Brainstorm ad concepts by listing two opposing ideas on either side of a page and writing the argument between them.
cards.use_when: You need a fresh static ad or landing page angle and your current drafts are flat feature lists.

cards.title: Drafting By 'Bleeding The Ink Dry' — Spitball Then Curate
cards.summary: Generate a large volume of rough candidate lines without judging them, then select and refine down through many rewrites.
cards.use_when: You are stuck on a headline, hook or hero line and every draft you produce is either obvious or precious.

cards.title: Build An Argument, Not A Claim — Small Believable Promises
cards.summary: Frame ads as arguments that move the buyer from a current to a desired belief, with modest believable claims rather than big hype.
cards.use_when: You are writing the hero section, email or paid ad for a conversion offer and want the claim to be credible rather than oversized.

cards.title: Positioning By Replacement And Smarter-Choice Framing
cards.summary: Define the product by what it replaces and by the smart, self-flattering decision it lets the buyer make.
cards.use_when: Your product is one of many similar options or has an obvious cheaper alternative, and you need a positioning line for PDP or ad creative.

cards.title: The One-Element Ad — Strip To The Essential Component
cards.summary: Reduce an ad to a single powerful element rather than the default header + subheader + picture + logo, if the single element can carry the message.
cards.use_when: You are designing static ads or PDP hero blocks with too much going on and want to increase stopping power.

cards.title: Storytelling With Cultural Scaffolding, Not Mascots
cards.summary: Let imagery lean on shared cultural references the audience already holds instead of inventing mascots that fit an unrelated category tone.
cards.use_when: You are choosing the hero image or creative concept for a brand whose promise is serious and where a mascot or gimmick would clash.

cards.title: Copy As Positioning: The Same Product, Sold Differently
cards.summary: Copy and branding can move identical commodities into completely different sales outcomes by positioning them differently.
cards.use_when: Your product is functionally similar to cheaper alternatives (commodity categories, private label comparisons) and you need a reason to exist beyond features.

cards.title: Metonymy — Swap Literal Category Words For Visual Ones
cards.summary: Replace a literal category label in copy with a concrete, surprising stand-in that is more visual and memorable.
cards.use_when: Your PDP or ad copy uses category words ('device', 'subscription plan', 'storage') that read flat and you need a line that sticks.

cards.title: Contrast and Juxtaposition As The Engine Of Memorability
cards.summary: Build memorable lines by putting two opposing ideas, numbers or images side by side and letting the tension do the work.
cards.use_when: You are writing a headline, subject line or hero copy and want it to stick without hype.

cards.title: If Possible: Publish Sourced Feedback Loops In Ad Production
cards.summary: Route finished ad copy through a small circle of trusted-taste reviewers before shipping, especially after long drafting sessions.
cards.use_when: You have been writing the same ad, subject line or hero for hours and can't judge whether it's good; you have trusted colleagues or peers available.

cards.title: Lead with facts instead of adjectives for ad and landing copy
cards.summary: Replace vague adjectives and opinions with specific, verifiable facts to make ad copy and product claims carry weight.
cards.use_when: Writing or auditing headline, PDP or ad copy where current claims feel vague ('high quality', 'unequal', 'sloppy') and you need credibility.

cards.title: Structure a newsletter with five to six dense examples and built-in conflict
cards.summary: Harry Dry's newsletter formula: five to six concrete examples per issue, each containing conflict, written in short paragraphs.
cards.use_when: Planning an email newsletter, retention email or content send for an ecommerce audience where engagement matters more than list size.

cards.title: Keep paragraphs to two lines and let each one earn its place
cards.summary: Short paragraphs help distracted readers move through copy, and force sharper self-editing.
cards.use_when: Formatting email, PDP or landing-page body copy that readers will skim on mobile or in a feed.

cards.title: Write simply by rewriting, not by trying to write simply the first time
cards.summary: Simplicity comes from repeated rewriting — write several versions of the same line and pick the best pieces.
cards.use_when: Drafting a headline, tagline or hero copy for a PDP or ad and the first pass feels clunky.

cards.title: Use 'and' as a red flag when scoping a product or brand
cards.summary: The strength of an idea is inversely proportional to its scope — 'and' on a landing page usually signals a diluted offer.
cards.use_when: Writing landing pages, brand taglines or collection descriptions and deciding what the store or product actually stands for.

cards.title: Structure copy by dividing it into named, parallel parts
cards.summary: Structure equals dividing lines plus parallelism — split a big idea into two or three labelled parts readers can hold onto.
cards.use_when: Writing a long-form sales page, PDP story, category page or ad narrative that currently feels like a wall of text.

cards.title: Hold a high quality bar and never let it fall — ship only 9/10 work
cards.summary: Your work is your standards: define what 'good' looks like and refuse to publish anything below it.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether a product page, ad, email or creative is ready to ship, especially under deadline pressure.

cards.title: Build conflict into ad creative using the implicit 'but'
cards.summary: Conflict (before/after, problem/solution, us-vs-them) makes messages memorable because humans remember relatively.
cards.use_when: Writing ad hooks, product stories or comparison sections where the copy reads flat and factual.

cards.title: Build a fact arsenal from first-hand experience, not invented detail
cards.summary: Writers like Ogilvy, Bukowski and Plath produced memorable work because they had direct experience of their subject — taste and conviction come from lived observation.
cards.use_when: Deciding what product details, founder stories or category observations to feature in your ad or PDP copy.

cards.title: Use AI as a tool, but judge output by your taste and conviction
cards.summary: AI can assist research and drafting, but has no taste, no belief and no lived experience — your standards decide whether its output is good.
cards.use_when: Deciding how to use AI in writing PDP copy, ad copy or newsletters without producing generic output.

cards.title: Protect silence and focus before writing sessions
cards.summary: Starting the day with silence and a walk rather than a feed improves the quality of writing work.
cards.use_when: Scheduling time to write ad copy, product pages or a newsletter that actually needs to be good.

cards.title: Treat Every Ad as a Salesman Held to Sales Standards
cards.summary: Judge advertising by whether it would help a real salesperson close a sale, not by whether it entertains or wins applause.
cards.use_when: Evaluating or briefing any ecommerce ad creative (Meta, TikTok, Google, email), or arbitrating disagreements about a headline, slogan or image in a campaign.

cards.title: Write the Headline to Hail Only the Interested Segment
cards.summary: A headline's job is to pick out the specific subset of readers who can be interested in the product and address them directly.
cards.use_when: Writing or testing headlines for an ecommerce ad, PDP hero, email subject line or landing page, where you must attract the right buyer rather than maximize raw clicks.

cards.title: Replace Superlatives With Specific, Verifiable Claims
cards.summary: General claims and superlatives are discounted by readers; a precise number or process earns full weight.
cards.use_when: Writing PDP copy, ad copy, offer claims or comparison copy where you need a claim to be believed rather than dismissed as hype.

cards.title: Lead With Service, Not a Buy Request
cards.summary: Offers that give the buyer something (trial, sample, useful information, risk-free approval) outsell ads that simply ask for the order.
cards.use_when: Designing an offer or acquisition creative for a hard-to-sell product, cold audience or high-consideration purchase where a direct 'buy now' ask is underperforming.

cards.title: Tell the Full Story in One Ad — No Serials
cards.summary: Once you have a reader's attention, present every important claim in that single ad; do not split arguments across a series.
cards.use_when: Structuring ad copy, PDP or landing page content where you must decide how much of the argument to include and whether to serialise messaging across multiple touchpoints.

cards.title: Use Mail-Order Discipline as the Benchmark for All Ads
cards.summary: Ads that sell goods by direct response are the severest test of copy and a model for economy of space, pictures and words.
cards.use_when: Reviewing whether your ecommerce ad creative is wasting budget on decoration, big type or design quirks, or when you lack any keyed results to judge an ad by.

cards.title: Key and Trace Ads to Replace Guesswork With Fixed Principles
cards.summary: Repeated keyed tests, watched at cost-per-reply and cost-per-sale, convert advertising from gambling into a science with reusable laws.
cards.use_when: Setting up an experiment cadence for ecommerce ad creative, PDP tests, headline tests or offer tests, and deciding what metric to judge them on.

cards.title: Apply Fixed Psychological Levers That Still Drive Buying
cards.summary: Human nature is stable, so curiosity, price-as-quality signals, personal ownership and class-restricted offers can be used deliberately to lift response.
cards.use_when: Designing ad angles, offer framing or PDP persuasion elements for an ecommerce product, notably when the product's real qualities are similar to competitors'.

cards.title: Use the Questionable Persona or Trusted Neighbour as the Seller
cards.summary: Attributing the offer to a credible human — a photographed, named dealer or a woman customers identify with — can beat an impersonal business offer.
cards.use_when: Building the 'from' identity for ecommerce ads, email, WhatsApp or DMs, especially for credit, instalment or higher-risk categories where trust is the barrier.

cards.title: Budget Ads Around Proven Claims, Not Around the Seller's Taste
cards.summary: The appeals you personally prefer rarely perform best, because you do not know enough people to average out their desires.
cards.use_when: Deciding which ad angles and headlines to scale in an ecommerce campaign, especially when your personal favourite is underperforming and a plain or surprising angle is winning.

cards.title: Judge Pictures by Their Selling Cost, Not Their Charm
cards.summary: Pictures consume one-third to one-half of many campaign budgets, so each must earn its space through tested selling power.
cards.use_when: Approving or cutting images in ecommerce ad creative, PDP galleries or landing pages when deciding whether an image justifies its place and cost.

cards.title: Interview and Sell to Buyers Before Writing Copy
cards.summary: Direct contact with prospective customers reveals the arguments and approaches that actually land, replacing expensive guesswork.
cards.use_when: Preparing copy for a product launch or a stalled ecommerce campaign where you have no reliable data on what buyers respond to.

cards.title: Use Test Campaigns to Set Spend Before Scaling
cards.summary: Small, keyed and traced tests establish which method pays before a full campaign commits ad budget.
cards.use_when: Planning the launch sequence and media budget for a new ecommerce product, market or creative concept before scaling spend.

cards.title: Let Data Decide When Craft and Storytelling Pay
cards.summary: Every departure from tested direct-response economy has a measurable price; keep it only if you knowingly accept that cost.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to invest in brand-style or design-led ecommerce creative versus plain, response-driven creative, and when defending or cutting costly creative elements.

cards.title: Only trust ads you can trace
cards.summary: Judge every ad, creative choice and offer by keyed returns, never by opinion or imitation of untraced advertising.
cards.use_when: Choosing ad creative, headlines or offers for any campaign and deciding whose advice to follow.

cards.title: Make your product its own best salesman with samples
cards.summary: Use samples not as giveaways but as interest filters that generate keyed prospects, cheaper follow-up and a fair product test.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether and how to run a sampling or trial offer for a physical product before scaling acquisition.

cards.title: Deliver samples where people already shop
cards.summary: Local sample delivery at stores drastically reduces inquiry cost versus mail, and simultaneously builds distribution.
cards.use_when: Structuring a sample or coupon offer and choosing between mail fulfilment, phone response and local store redemption.

cards.title: Use test campaigns to answer selling questions before you scale
cards.summary: Prove a new product, form, price or method in a few towns, measure cost and repeat purchase, then roll out with known economics.
cards.use_when: Launching a new product, new campaign or major creative change, or deciding whether to scale national spend.

cards.title: Judge a product by whether repeat sales repay acquisition cost
cards.summary: Before scaling, establish cost per customer, revenue per customer and payback time; short-lived, one-purchase items often can't be advertised profitably.
cards.use_when: Deciding whether to advertise a new product, setting allowable acquisition cost, or comparing products for portfolio investment.

cards.title: Don't spend to educate a habit you can't own
cards.summary: Changing consumer habits is prohibitive for one advertiser; watch trends created by others and move in to satisfy demand at the right time.
cards.use_when: Evaluating a campaign that tries to create a new consumer habit, category or education objective rather than satisfy existing demand.

cards.title: Pick the claim that appeals to the most buyers
cards.summary: When a product has several true claims, feature the one with the widest appeal in headlines and relegate niche claims to body copy or occasional ads.
cards.use_when: Writing headlines and PDP copy for a product with multiple benefits, especially health, cosmetic or functional claims.

cards.title: Research the product exhaustively before writing
cards.summary: Weeks of reading, consumer canvassing and dealer research often surface the single fact that becomes the campaign's keystone.
cards.use_when: Preparing to write ad or PDP copy for a new product or entering a category you don't know well.

cards.title: Choose names and prices as strategy, not afterthoughts
cards.summary: Names that tell a story or create an exclusive category, and prices matched to volume versus margin needs, shape an entire campaign.
cards.use_when: Naming a product or line extension, and setting or repositioning price before advertising.

cards.title: Map the competitive field before choosing your angle
cards.summary: Study entrenched rivals' price, quality and claims, and find a real, tellable advantage that gives satisfied users a reason to switch.
cards.use_when: Entering an established category or launching against entrenched brands, and deciding whether to attack, differentiate or avoid the fight.

cards.title: Get distribution before or alongside advertising
cards.summary: Advertising before availability wastes converts; use sample and coupon offers naming specific dealers to force stock and achieve distribution quickly.
cards.use_when: Running any campaign where consumers must be able to buy immediately after seeing the ad.

cards.title: Don't buy dealer effort; buy customers
cards.summary: Dealer help, loading discounts and displays often shift sales between stores rather than growing total sales — spend that money on creating customers instead.
cards.use_when: Evaluating trade discounts, loading offers, display allowances and display placement as a route to sales growth.

cards.title: Positive ads beat negative appeals
cards.summary: Show the desired outcome and the envied life, not the problem or the afflicted customer; Hopkins claims positive ads pull four to one over negative ones.
cards.use_when: Choosing imagery, headlines and proof points for ads, PDP hero images or landing pages for beauty, health, apparel, education or self-improvement products.

cards.title: Keep a consistent advertising personality
cards.summary: Give your advertising a consistent, distinctive personality and don't change what has proved appealing; readers build confidence through repeated acquaintance.
cards.use_when: Setting tone of voice for an ongoing campaign and onboarding new writers or agencies who produce ad and PDP copy.

cards.title: Make pictures argue only when letters wouldn't pay better
cards.summary: Pictures are often a third to a half of the campaign stake, so use them only when they out-sell the same space in type, and never merely to attract attention.
cards.use_when: Allocating space between imagery and copy in ads or on PDP and landing pages, and deciding art style.
